policy: Review every closed candidate set. Select only when ASV wording or an explicit mapped textual note distinguishes a reading; otherwise mark underdetermined and retain the base fallback. The base candidate is the SBLGNT reading.

decisions.evidence: ASV renders the interrogative twice, "Whence come wars and whence come fightings"; the omitting reading leaves nothing for the second "whence".
ASV opens "Ye adulteresses" alone, with no masculine counterpart; the longer reading would require "Ye adulterers and adulteresses".
ἐὰν and ἂν are orthographic variants of the same generalising particle with ὃς; ASV's "Whosoever therefore would be" renders either identically.

ASV text reads "the spirit which he made to dwell in us" (causative κατῴκισεν), and the textual_variant note assigns the intransitive "dwelleth in us" (κατῴκησεν) to some ancient authorities, i.e. not to the text.
ἐγγιεῖ and ἐγγίσει are alternate future forms of the same verb; "he will draw nigh to you" renders either.
μετατραπήτω and μεταστραφήτω are synonymous aorist passive imperatives; "let your laughter be turned" distinguishes neither.
The variant is the presence of the article with κυρίou; English "the Lord" is required either way and cannot distinguish it.
ASV reads "speaketh against a brother, or judgeth his brother" — disjunctive ἢ, not the connective καί.
The variant adds only the article before νομοθέτης; ASV's "One only is the lawgiver" supplies "the" as ordinary English predicate-noun definiteness and settles nothing.
ASV has "the lawgiver and judge"; the omitting reading leaves no κριτής for "and judge".
ASV "who art thou that judgest thy neighbor?" fits both the participial ὁ κρίvων and the relative clause ὃς κρίvεις, which English renders alike with "that judgest".
ASV reads "thy neighbor" (πλησίoν), not "another" (ἕτερον).
ASV reads "To-day or to-morrow" — disjunctive ἢ, not καί.
ASV "we will go into this city" is future indicative reported speech; the hortatory subjunctive πορευσῴμεθα would give "let us go".
"and spend a year there" continues the future indicative "we will" of the same clause chain; the subjunctive ποιήσωμεν would give "let us spend".
ASV "a year" renders ἐνιαυτόν with or without ἕνα, which idiomatic English takes as the indefinite article rather than as "one year".
"and trade" continues the future indicative "we will"; the subjunctive ἐμπορευσῴμεθα would give "let us trade".
"and get gain" continues the future indicative "we will"; the subjunctive κερδήσωμεν would give "let us get gain".
The variant is the presence of the neuter article in τὸ τῆς αὔριον; ASV's "what shall be on the morrow" paraphrases the phrase either way.
ASV asks "What is your life?" with no connective, and places "For" with the following γάρ clause ("For ye are a vapor"); the added γάρ would require "For what is your life".
ASV reads second person plural "ye are a vapor" (ἐστε), not the third person singular "it shall be" of ἔσται.
The variant is only the article with ζωή; ASV's possessive "your life" requires no determiner distinction and settles nothing.
ASV's "and then vanisheth away" uses "and" as the ordinary English link between coordinate clauses, which neither requires nor excludes an added δέ.
θελήσῃ and θέλῃ are aorist and present subjunctive of the same verb in the same condition; "If the Lord will" renders either.
ASV "we shall both live" is future indicative ζήσομεν; the subjunctive ζήσωμεν would give "let us live".
"and do this or that" continues the future indicative "we shall"; the subjunctive ποιήσωμεν would give "let us do".
